## EC Summary Requirements

#### 1. Changes with respect to the DoA

The work carried out under this task closely aligns with what was described in the DoA with the following adaptations.

The cross-country Europea-wide mapping of advisory body design features set out in the DoA was completed and informed the selection of case studies for this report. It is not reproduced in full in order to keep this deliverable focused, but a summary table is presented on p.10. The DoA proposed three national case studies, each assessing set-up, governance, mandate, and key outputs. This report instead presents three case studies covering four countries, each using a different method suited to the specific question it addresses (see p.13) but drawing on analysis of references to the bodies in policy reports and decisions, parliamentary debates, and major media outlets as set out in the DoA.

The DoA specified at least 10 semi-structured interviews with members of advisory bodies, experts from government, parliament, civil society and business organisations. The first (Section 4) and third (Section 6) case study draw on 23 interviews in total, exceeding this minimum. The selection of interviewees was slightly adapted in light of access and relevance, with more academics and media actors interviewed in the place of businesses representatives, but represented a broad range of stakeholders consistent with the DoA.

#### 2. Dissemination and uptake

This deliverable is for publication for the wider public and for use within the project consortium.

#### 3. Short summary of results (<250 words)

This report, produced under Work Package 4 of the RETOOL project, examines the contribution of independent climate advisory bodies to democratic climate governance. Over 40 countries have established such bodies, yet existing research skews toward the UK’s Committee on Climate Change (CCC). It emphasises positive impact on climate policymaking but does not address the impact on broader democratic governance and does not consider how these bodies withstand growing political contestation around climate action across Europe.

The report addresses these gaps in two ways. First, applying the RETOOL analytical framework, it evaluates the impact of Ireland’s Climate Change Advisory Council (CCAC) across the pillars of climate democracy. Second, it examines how advisory bodies are impacted by and respond to rising contestation—externally, through UK CCC mentions in parliamentary debate, and internally, through interviews with policy stakeholders in Ireland, Finland and Sweden and the Irish CCAC, the Finnish Climate Change Panel, and the Swedish Climate Policy Council.

Findings show that the advisory bodies considered in the study contribute most strongly to the effectiveness and accountability pillars of climate democracy, while their contribution to participation and deliberativeness remains limited, except for the UK CCC, largely due to mandate and resourcing constraints rather than any inherent limitation of the model. Under political contestation, institutional resilience depends less on public standing of the body than on statutory embeddedness, parliamentary engagement, and anchoring to legal commitments such as EU targets. A statutory “duty to respond” requiring governments to consider and respond to advice matters for impact but is not sufficient alone. The report concludes with recommendations on legal embeddedness, mandate and accountability provisions, funding arrangements and strategies for the bodies to increase resilience.

#### 4. Evidence of accomplishment

This report.

## Preface

The overall goal of the RETOOL project is to advance our understanding of how to address the twin challenges of responding to the climate imperative while strengthening and reinvigorating democratic governance. The project has four overarching objectives: (i) To deepen our understanding of the relationship between democratic governance and the climate imperative by developing a novel analytical framework and creating new empirical underpinnings, including important new open-access datasets; (ii) To understand how a variety of democratic institutions across Europe are responding to the climate challenge, including learning lessons from history and studying new and innovative democratic practices; (iii) To contribute to reinvigorating democratic governance in Europe by developing and synthesising new knowledge and insights on climate democracy, and presenting them in a range of high-impact formats; and (iv) To serve as a bridge between academic research on climate democracy innovations and policymakers and practitioners, as well as civil society and the wider public. RETOOL brings together an international and interdisciplinary consortium, with partners from Western Europe (Ireland, UK, Belgium, Austria), Northern Europe (Finland), Eastern Europe (Estonia), and Southern Europe (Italy, Greece), combining expertise in political science, political sociology, deliberative democracy, environmental law, European studies, and public administration. The consortium includes a democracy practitioner foundation (Praxis), and all partners are closely associated with practitioner and civil society networks and involved in hands-on activities. RETOOL will be undertaken by a mature, settled consortium that has significant experience of working together, with six of our nine partners core members of the EU-funded Jean Monnet Network GreenDeal-NET.

## Executive Summary

Background and rationale: This report, produced under Work Package 4 of the RETOOL project, examines the contribution of independent climate advisory bodies—expert councils, committees, or panels—to democratic climate governance. Over 40 countries have established such bodies as a cornerstone of climate governance, yet existing research skews toward the UK’s Committee on Climate Change (CCC), emphasises policy impact over broader governance contribution, and rarely addresses how these bodies withstand growing political contestation around climate action.

Objectives and approach: The report addresses these gaps in two ways. First, applying the RETOOL analytical framework that outlines key features of democratic climate governance, it evaluates the impact of Ireland’s Climate Change Advisory Council (CCAC) across the pillars of climate democracy, drawing on 15 stakeholder interviews. Second, it examines how advisory bodies are affected by, and respond to, rising political contestation—externally, through analysis of UK CCC mentions in parliamentary debate between 2019 and 2025, and internally, through 23 interviews with members, secretariats, and external stakeholders of the Irish CCAC, the Finnish Ilmastopaneeli (Climate Change Panel) and the Swedish Klimatpolitiska Rådet (Climate Policy Council).

Key findings: Independent advisory bodies make their strongest and most consistent contribution to the effectiveness and accountability pillars of climate democracy, through their influence on carbon budgets, targets, and policy measures, and through their watchdog function. Their contribution to participation and deliberativeness remains limited, a gap attributed primarily to mandate and resourcing constraints rather than any inherent limitation of the advisory-body model. Under political contestation, institutional resilience depends less on public popularity than on statutory embeddedness, parliamentary engagement, and anchoring to external commitments such as EU targets; a statutory “duty to respond” matters for impact but is not sufficient on its own, as the comparison with Denmark’s stronger “duty to act” model shows. Advisory bodies have adopted a range of adaptive strategies in response to contestation, spanning communication practice, stakeholder engagement, and collaboration with sister bodies—though resourcing constraints run through nearly all of them, leaving their ultimate resilience dependent on political will in the absence of stronger institutional safeguards.

Recommendations: The report sets out recommendations in four areas. On establishment and legal embeddedness, it recommends embedding advisory bodies and their core mandates directly in legislation, with statutory funding floors, multi-year funding cycles, and cross-party input into appointments. On mandate design, it recommends moving towards a statutory duty to act rather than merely to respond, explicitly authorising public engagement and stakeholder consultation, and providing a legal right of access to government data. For advisory bodies themselves, it recommends diversified communication practices, deliberate stakeholder-ecosystem building, joint publications with sister bodies, and proactively building an evidence base of their own cost-effectiveness.
